introduction-why-go-is-an-ops-superpower.core: Go compiles to a single static binary, has cheap built-in concurrency and runs fast. That's why Kubernetes, Docker, Terraform and Prometheus are written in it.

first_principles.problem: Python tools need interpreters and dependencies on every host, and they struggle with thousands of concurrent network calls.
truths: Distributing a runtime is painful.
Ops tools are network- and concurrency-heavy.
The cloud-native ecosystem speaks Go.
derivation: **Single binary**: copy it and run it.
**Static typing** catches errors at compile time.
You can read the **source of your infra tools**.

analogy.title: A self-contained camping stove
analogy.story: It comes with everything inside: no gas line (runtime) to install at each campsite (server).
analogy.breaks: Go is more verbose than Python for quick data munging; use each where it fits.

example.title: Health-checking 500 servers
flow: Ship one binary to the bastion
example.outcome: Go is the natural choice for distributed ops tools.

check.q: Why is a static binary valuable for ops?
check.a: It runs anywhere without installing a runtime or dependencies.

go-basics-the-building-blocks-you-need-f.core: Go has packages and imports, a `main` entry point, typed variables (`:=` infers the type), functions with multiple returns, structs, slices, maps and for loops. That's enough to read most ops code.

first_principles.problem: The later concurrency and JSON lessons are unreadable without the basic syntax.
truths: Go deliberately has a small set of features.
Every file belongs to a package.
Types are explicit or inferred.
derivation: Use **slices** for lists, **maps** for dicts, and **for** as the only loop.

analogy.title: Learning the alphabet before writing
analogy.story: A small alphabet (few keywords) and you can read every sentence.
analogy.breaks: Go's minimalism means some things (generics, enums) feel different from other languages.

example.title: A tiny program
example.outcome: you can read and write simple Go.

check.q: What is Go's only loop keyword?
check.a: for (it also covers while and range loops).

concurrency-goroutines.core: Prefixing a call with `go` runs it as a goroutine, a lightweight concurrent task of a few KB. Use a `sync.WaitGroup` to wait for them all to finish.

first_principles.problem: Checking 200 servers one at a time with a 5 s timeout takes up to 1,000 seconds.
truths: I/O waits dominate ops work.
OS threads are expensive; goroutines are cheap.
You have to know when concurrent work has finished.

analogy.title: Sending many letters at once
analogy.story: Instead of waiting for each reply before sending the next letter, post them all and wait for the replies together.
analogy.breaks: Unbounded goroutines can overwhelm targets or run out of file descriptors, so limit concurrency.

example.title: 200 health checks in parallel

steps.label: Result
steps.detail: Runtime is bounded by the slowest host.

example.outcome: massive I/O parallelism with little code.

check.a: Blocks until every goroutine that called Add has called Done.

concurrency-channels.core: Channels are typed pipes between goroutines: they send results safely without shared memory or locks. 'Don't communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating.'

first_principles.problem: Goroutines writing to one shared variable cause race conditions unless you lock carefully.
truths: Shared mutable state with concurrency is error-prone.
Message passing transfers ownership.
An unbuffered send blocks until it's received.
derivation: **Buffered** channels decouple the speed of producer and consumer.

analogy.title: A pneumatic tube system
analogy.story: Workers drop results in the tube; the receiver takes them out one at a time. No-one fights over a shared desk.
analogy.breaks: Sending on a channel nobody reads from blocks forever, which is a goroutine leak.

example.title: Collecting health results
example.scenario: Each goroutine sends its result back.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No locks and no races, and results arrive as they finish.

check.q: What happens when you send on an unbuffered channel no-one reads?
check.a: The sender blocks forever, which leaks the goroutine.

concurrency-select-and-context-timeouts.core: `select` waits on several channel operations at once; `context` carries deadlines and cancellation. Together they ensure nothing in an ops tool waits forever.

first_principles.problem: A health check against a black-holed host hangs indefinitely and freezes the whole tool.
truths: Networks can stall forever.
Work should stop when its caller gives up.
You often wait on 'result or timeout'.

analogy.title: An egg timer during cooking
analogy.story: You wait for the dish or the timer, whichever comes first. When the timer rings, you stop.
analogy.breaks: Cancellation only works if downstream code actually checks ctx.

example.title: A 5-second health check

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Dead hosts fail after 5 s instead of hanging.

code.text:
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 5*time.Second)
defer cancel()
req, _ := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, "GET", url, nil)
resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req) // errors after 5s

example.outcome: every operation has a bounded wait.

check.q: Why pass ctx to downstream calls?
check.a: So their work is cancelled when the deadline passes or the caller gives up.

resource-cleanup-the-defer-keyword.core: `defer` schedules a call to run when the function returns, on every exit path. Placing `defer f.Close()` right after opening guarantees the cleanup happens.

first_principles.problem: Functions with several early error returns forget to close files or connections, leaking file descriptors.
truths: Functions have many exit paths.
Every resource you acquire must be released.
Code next to its pair is easier to verify.
derivation: Acquire, check the error, then **defer release** immediately.

analogy.title: Writing 'turn off the oven' on the door
analogy.story: Whatever path you take out of the kitchen, the note is on the door you leave through.
analogy.breaks: A defer inside a long loop only runs at function exit, so resources pile up until then.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No FD leaks, even with five early returns.

check.q: In what order do multiple defers run?

parsing-json-with-structs.core: Unmarshal JSON into typed structs whose field tags map JSON keys. Mistyped or missing fields become compile-time types or zero values instead of runtime surprises.

first_principles.problem: Accessing nested map keys by string works until a typo or type change causes a runtime crash.
truths: APIs return JSON with a known shape.
Typed fields catch misuse at compile time.
Tags decouple Go names from JSON names.
derivation: Use **omitempty** and pointers for optional fields.

analogy.title: A pre-labelled form
analogy.story: Data is poured into labelled boxes; anything that doesn't fit a box is noticed.
analogy.breaks: Unknown fields are silently ignored by default. Use DisallowUnknownFields for strictness.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: pods[0].Ready is a bool, and the compiler checks how you use it.

check.q: What do struct tags like `json:"name"` do?
check.a: They map the Go field to a specific JSON key.

interfaces-implicit-implementation.core: A Go interface is a set of methods. Any type with those methods satisfies it automatically, with no `implements` keyword, which makes swapping implementations (for example in tests) trivial.

first_principles.problem: Hard-coding a concrete AWS client makes code untestable without real cloud calls.
truths: Code should depend on behaviour, not concrete types.
Small interfaces are easy to satisfy.
Implicit satisfaction keeps packages decoupled.
derivation: Define a **small interface** where it's used (e.g. `Notifier { Send(msg) error }`).
Inject the **real one in prod and a fake in tests**.

analogy.title: A wall socket
analogy.story: Anything with the right plug works: a lamp or a phone charger. The socket doesn't care what's behind the plug.
analogy.breaks: Interfaces defined too early or too large add abstraction without benefit.

example.title: Swappable alerting
example.scenario: Slack in production, a fake in tests.

steps.label: Test
steps.detail: Pass a fakeNotifier that records messages, so no network is needed.

check.q: How does a Go type implement an interface?
check.a: Simply by having all the interface's methods; no declaration is needed.

error-handling-patterns.core: Go errors are ordinary return values that you check immediately. Wrap them with `%w` to add context, and inspect them with errors.Is or errors.As. Failure handling stays visible and explicit.

first_principles.problem: Exceptions can bubble up invisibly, and bare errors like 'file not found' give no clue which file or why.
truths: Failures are normal in ops code.
Context matters for debugging.
Callers need to tell error types apart.
derivation: Write **`if err != nil { return ... }`** right after the call.
**errors.Is** for sentinel errors and **errors.As** for typed ones.
Use **panic** only for truly impossible states.

analogy.title: Breadcrumbs on a trail
analogy.story: Each layer adds a breadcrumb, so you can retrace exactly where things went wrong.
analogy.breaks: Verbose `if err != nil` checks are the price you pay for explicitness.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The log line says exactly what failed and where.

check.a: %w keeps the original error so errors.Is and errors.As can still match it.

binaries-cross-compilation-and-static-li.core: Setting GOOS and GOARCH cross-compiles for any platform from your laptop, and CGO_ENABLED=0 produces a fully static binary that runs in a scratch container or on any Linux box.

first_principles.problem: Deploying a Python tool to 300 mixed servers means managing interpreters and packages on each one.
truths: Most runtimes must be installed on the target.
Static binaries carry their dependencies.
Small images reduce attack surface.
derivation: Run **`GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64 go build`** for any target.

analogy.title: A pre-assembled flat-pack, ready to use
analogy.story: No assembly or extra screws needed at the destination; you just set it down.
analogy.breaks: Programs that need cgo (some DNS or SQLite cases) can't always be fully static.

steps.label: Deploy
steps.detail: Copy one file to each server, or put it in a 10 MB scratch image.

code.text:
CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 go build -o bin/tool-linux-amd64
GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64 go build -o bin/tool-linux-arm64
GOOS=windows go build -o bin/tool.exe

check.a: A pure-Go static binary with no libc dependency, so it runs anywhere.
